name: abs
summary: Absolute value of a number
description: Returns `value` with its sign removed, so the result is never negative. NaN stays NaN.

name: acos
summary: Arc cosine, in degrees
description: Returns the angle, in **degrees** (0 to 180), whose cosine is `value`. Input slightly outside -1..1 (a rounding near-miss such as 1.0005) is treated as the nearest endpoint instead of producing NaN.

args.name: value
args.description: Cosine of the angle, normally -1 to 1.

notes: Returns degrees, not radians — unlike most programming languages.
Inputs just outside -1..1 are pulled to the endpoint rather than returning NaN; don't rely on this for values far outside the range.
Results are float32, so right angles come out a few ulps off (e.g. 90.00001).

name: asin
summary: Arc sine, in degrees
description: Returns the angle, in **degrees** (-90 to 90), whose sine is `value`. Input slightly outside -1..1 is treated as the nearest endpoint instead of producing NaN.

args.name: value
args.description: Sine of the angle, normally -1 to 1.

notes: Returns degrees, not radians.
Inputs just outside -1..1 are pulled to the endpoint rather than returning NaN; don't rely on this for values far outside the range.

name: atan
summary: Arc tangent, in degrees
description: Returns the angle, in **degrees** (between -90 and 90), whose tangent is `value`.
notes: Returns degrees, not radians.
Cannot tell opposite quadrants apart; use `math.atan2(y, x)` when you have both components.

name: atan2
summary: Angle of the vector (x, y) in degrees; y comes first
description: Returns the angle, in **degrees** (-180 to 180), from the positive x axis to the point (`x`, `y`). Note the argument order: `y` first, then `x`. `math.atan2(1, 0)` is 90 and `math.atan2(0, -1)` is 180.
notes: Argument order is (y, x), matching C's atan2 — swapping them silently gives the wrong angle.
Returns degrees, not radians.

name: ceil
summary: Round up to the nearest whole number
description: Returns the smallest whole number that is greater than or equal to `value`. `math.ceil(1.2)` is 2 and `math.ceil(-1.2)` is -1.

name: clamp
summary: Limit a value to the range min..max
description: Returns `value` limited to lie between `min` and `max`. The upper bound is checked first: anything above `max` becomes `max`, otherwise anything at or below `min` becomes `min`. If `value` is NaN, NaN is returned.
notes: Bounds are not swapped for you. With `min` greater than `max` the upper bound wins for large values: `math.clamp(3, 2, 1)` is 1 and `math.clamp(-2, -1, -3)` is -3.
A NaN value passes straight through.

name: copy_sign
summary: Magnitude of the first number with the sign of the second
description: Returns the absolute value of `value` carrying the sign of `sign`. A negative zero in `sign` counts as negative, so `math.copy_sign(3, -0)` is -3.

name: cos
summary: Cosine of an angle given in degrees
description: Returns the cosine of `angle`, where `angle` is in **degrees** (not radians). The result is between -1 and 1. The conversion to radians is done in single precision, so values that should be exactly zero are not: `math.cos(90)` is about -4.4e-8.
notes: Takes degrees, not radians — `math.cos(math.pi)` is the cosine of about 3.14 degrees, not -1.
Expected zeros come out as tiny non-zero values (`math.cos(90)` ≈ -4.4e-8), so avoid exact `== 0` comparisons.
The last bit can differ between platforms, since the game uses the device's C library for this.

name: die_roll
summary: Sum of several random decimal rolls in the range low..high
description: Rolls `count` times, each roll a random decimal between `low` and `high` (like `math.random`), and returns the sum. `count` is rounded to the nearest whole number; zero or a negative count returns 0 without rolling.

args.name: count
args.description: How many rolls to add together.

notes: The count comes FIRST: `math.die_roll(count, low, high)`, not `(low, high, count)`.
Each roll is a decimal, not a whole number — use `math.die_roll_integer` for dice-like values.
Consumes one random draw per roll; a large count is slow, as there is no upper limit.
Fields that refuse `math.random` (block permutation conditions, block bone visibility) do not refuse this, even though it is just as random.

name: die_roll_integer
summary: Sum of several random whole-number rolls, low..high inclusive
description: Rolls `count` times, each roll a random whole number from `low` to `high` inclusive (like `math.random_integer`), and returns the sum. `count` is rounded to the nearest whole number; zero or a negative count returns 0 without rolling.

args.name: count
args.description: How many rolls to add together.

notes: The count comes FIRST: `math.die_roll_integer(2, 1, 6)` is two six-sided dice.
Pass whole numbers: bounds are not rounded, so a fractional `low` shifts every roll by that fraction.
Keep `low` ≤ `high`; reversed bounds do not swap and produce meaningless (often huge) values.
Consumes one random draw per roll.
Fields that refuse `math.random_integer` (block permutation conditions, block bone visibility) do not refuse this, even though it is just as random.

name: ease_in_back
summary: Ease-in back easing from start to end
description: Interpolates from `start` to `end` along an overshooting curve that starts slowly and speeds up toward `end`. Returns `start + (end − start) × curve(t)`: `start` at t = 0 and `end` at t = 1. The curve pulls back behind `start` before moving.
notes: `t` is not clamped: values below 0 or above 1 extrapolate the curve. Clamp it yourself (`math.clamp(t, 0, 1)`) for a bounded result.
Argument order is (start, end, t) — the progress value comes last.
The result goes outside `start`..`end` by design: in variants dip below `start`, out variants overshoot `end`.

name: ease_in_bounce
summary: Ease-in bounce easing from start to end
description: Interpolates from `start` to `end` along a bouncing curve that starts slowly and speeds up toward `end`. Returns `start + (end − start) × curve(t)`: `start` at t = 0 and `end` at t = 1.
notes: `t` is not clamped: values below 0 or above 1 extrapolate the curve. Clamp it yourself (`math.clamp(t, 0, 1)`) for a bounded result.
Argument order is (start, end, t) — the progress value comes last.

name: ease_in_circ
summary: Ease-in circular easing from start to end
description: Interpolates from `start` to `end` along a circular-arc curve that starts slowly and speeds up toward `end`. Returns `start + (end − start) × curve(t)`: `start` at t = 0 and `end` at t = 1.
notes: `t` is not clamped: values below 0 or above 1 extrapolate the curve. Clamp it yourself (`math.clamp(t, 0, 1)`) for a bounded result.
Argument order is (start, end, t) — the progress value comes last.
Outside the range the circle is defined on, the result is NaN (e.g. `math.ease_in_circ(0, 1, 2)`), and NaN counts as true in conditions.

name: ease_in_cubic
summary: Ease-in cubic easing from start to end
description: Interpolates from `start` to `end` along a cubic curve, stronger than quad that starts slowly and speeds up toward `end`. Returns `start + (end − start) × curve(t)`: `start` at t = 0 and `end` at t = 1.
notes: `t` is not clamped: values below 0 or above 1 extrapolate the curve. Clamp it yourself (`math.clamp(t, 0, 1)`) for a bounded result.
Argument order is (start, end, t) — the progress value comes last.

name: ease_in_elastic
summary: Ease-in elastic easing from start to end
description: Interpolates from `start` to `end` along a springy, oscillating curve that starts slowly and speeds up toward `end`. Returns `start + (end − start) × curve(t)`: `start` at t = 0 and `end` at t = 1.
notes: `t` is not clamped: values below 0 or above 1 extrapolate the curve. Clamp it yourself (`math.clamp(t, 0, 1)`) for a bounded result.
Argument order is (start, end, t) — the progress value comes last.
The result goes outside `start`..`end` by design while oscillating.
Uses a 65536-step sine lookup table, so values are quantised; the endpoints themselves are exact.

name: ease_in_expo
summary: Ease-in exponential easing from start to end
description: Interpolates from `start` to `end` along a sharp exponential curve that starts slowly and speeds up toward `end`. Returns `start + (end − start) × curve(t)`: `start` at t = 0 and `end` at t = 1.
notes: `t` is not clamped: values below 0 or above 1 extrapolate the curve. Clamp it yourself (`math.clamp(t, 0, 1)`) for a bounded result.
Argument order is (start, end, t) — the progress value comes last.

The endpoints are not snapped: at t = 0 and t = 1 the result is very slightly off `start`/`end` (e.g. `math.ease_out_expo(0, 1, 1)` is 0.99902, `math.ease_in_expo(0, 1, 0)` is 0.00098). Don't compare to `end` exactly.

name: ease_in_out_back
summary: Ease-in-out back easing from start to end
description: Interpolates from `start` to `end` along an overshooting curve that starts slowly, speeds up in the middle and slows into `end`, symmetric around t = 0.5. Returns `start + (end − start) × curve(t)`: `start` at t = 0 and `end` at t = 1. The curve pulls back behind `start` and overshoots `end`.
notes: `t` is not clamped: values below 0 or above 1 extrapolate the curve. Clamp it yourself (`math.clamp(t, 0, 1)`) for a bounded result.
Argument order is (start, end, t) — the progress value comes last.
The result goes outside `start`..`end` by design: in variants dip below `start`, out variants overshoot `end`.

name: exp
summary: e raised to a power
description: Returns e (≈2.71828) raised to the power `value`. Overflows to infinity above roughly 88 and underflows to 0 for very negative input.
notes: float32 range is small: `math.exp(89)` is already infinity.

name: floor
summary: Round down to the nearest whole number
description: Returns the largest whole number that is less than or equal to `value`. `math.floor(1.7)` is 1 and `math.floor(-1.2)` is -2.
notes: Rounds toward negative infinity; use `math.trunc` to drop the fraction toward zero instead.
Beware tiny negative results from trig: `math.floor(math.sin(180))` is -1, not 0.

name: hermite_blend
summary: Smooth S-curve 3t² − 2t³
description: Returns `3t² − 2t³`, a smooth step that is 0 at t = 0, 0.5 at t = 0.5 and 1 at t = 1, with zero slope at both ends.
notes: `t` is not clamped: outside 0..1 the curve keeps going (`math.hermite_blend(2)` is -4). Clamp it yourself if needed.

name: inverse_lerp
summary: Where a value sits between start and end, as a 0..1 fraction
description: Returns `(value − start) / (end − start)`: 0 when `value` equals `start`, 1 when it equals `end`, and proportionally in between. Values outside the range give results below 0 or above 1.
notes: Not clamped: values beyond `start`..`end` give results outside 0..1.
Unlike the `/` operator, there is no divide-by-zero guard: when `start` equals `end` the result is ±infinity, or NaN if `value` equals them too.

name: lerp
summary: Linear interpolation from start to end
description: Returns `start + (end − start) × t`: `start` at t = 0, `end` at t = 1, halfway at 0.5.
notes: `t` is not clamped: `math.lerp(0, 10, 2)` is 20. Wrap it in `math.clamp(t, 0, 1)` if you need a bounded result.

name: lerprotate
summary: Interpolate between two angles the short way round
description: Interpolates from angle `start` to angle `end` (in **degrees**) by `t`, taking the shortest direction around the circle. `math.lerprotate(350, 10, 0.5)` moves 10° forward to 360 rather than 170° backward.
notes: The result is not wrapped into any range: it can land outside 0..360 or -180..180 (e.g. 360, or -90 for 0 → 270). Use `math.min_angle` to normalise it.
`t` is not clamped.

name: ln
summary: Natural logarithm
description: Returns the natural (base-e) logarithm of `value`. `math.ln(0)` is negative infinity and a negative input gives NaN.
notes: There is no log10 or log2; divide by `math.ln(10)` or `math.ln(2)`.

name: max
summary: The larger of two numbers
description: Returns whichever of `a` and `b` is greater.
notes: NaN handling depends on order: if either argument is NaN, the SECOND argument is returned. `math.max(NaN, 3)` is 3 but `math.max(3, NaN)` is NaN.

name: min
summary: The smaller of two numbers
description: Returns whichever of `a` and `b` is smaller.
notes: NaN handling depends on order: if either argument is NaN, the SECOND argument is returned. `math.min(NaN, 3)` is 3 but `math.min(3, NaN)` is NaN.

name: min_angle
summary: Wrap an angle into the range -180..180 degrees
description: Returns the equivalent angle in **degrees** within -180 to 180, e.g. `math.min_angle(370)` is 10 and `math.min_angle(190)` is -170.
notes: An input of exactly ±180 (or an odd multiple of it) may come back as either 180 or -180; don't compare the result to one of them exactly.

name: mod
summary: Remainder of a division, keeping the sign of the dividend
description: Returns the remainder of `value / divisor`. The result has the sign of `value` (like C's fmod): `math.mod(-7, 3)` is -1, not 2. Division by zero returns 0 rather than NaN.
notes: Molang has no `%` operator; this is the only modulo.
Negative inputs give negative remainders. For a wrap-around index use `math.mod(math.mod(v.i, n) + n, n)`.
`math.mod(x, 0)` is 0.

name: pi
summary: The constant π (≈3.1415927)
description: The value of π rounded to single precision, 3.1415927. It is a value, not a function: write `math.pi`, not `math.pi()`.
notes: Molang's trig functions take and return degrees, so you rarely need π for them: `math.sin(90)` is 1, while `math.sin(math.pi)` is the sine of 3.14 degrees.

name: pow
summary: Raise a number to a power
description: Returns `base` raised to `exponent`. A negative base with a fractional exponent gives NaN, and 0 to a negative power gives infinity.
notes: `math.pow(-8, 1/3)` is NaN, not -2.
The last bit can differ between platforms, since the game uses the device's C library for this.

name: random
summary: Random decimal between low and high
description: Returns a random decimal number from `low` up to (but, apart from rounding, not including) `high`. Each call draws a new value. `low` and `high` may be given in either order.
notes: Not an integer picker: `math.random(1, 6)` returns values like 3.8127. Use `math.random_integer` for whole numbers.
Contexts that disallow random numbers (block permutation conditions, block bone visibility) refuse expressions that call it.

name: random_integer
summary: Random whole number from low to high, both inclusive
description: Returns a random whole number from `low` to `high`, **including both ends**, so `math.random_integer(1, 6)` behaves like a six-sided die. When `low` equals `high` that value is returned.
notes: Both bounds are inclusive — unlike most languages' random-int functions.
Pass whole numbers: bounds are not rounded, so `math.random_integer(0.5, 3)` returns 0.5, 1.5 or 2.5.
Keep `low` ≤ `high`; reversed bounds do not swap and produce meaningless (often huge) values.
Contexts that disallow random numbers (block permutation conditions, block bone visibility) refuse expressions that call it.

name: round
summary: Round to the nearest whole number, halves away from zero
description: Returns `value` rounded to the nearest whole number. Exact halves round away from zero: `math.round(2.5)` is 3 and `math.round(-2.5)` is -3.
notes: Halves go away from zero, not to the nearest even number.

name: sign
summary: 1 for zero or positive input, -1 for negative input
description: Returns -1 if `value` is negative and 1 otherwise. Zero counts as positive, so `math.sign(0)` is **1**, never 0.
notes: Never returns 0: testing `math.sign(v.x) == 0` never matches, and multiplying by it will not zero anything out.
Negative zero and NaN also give 1.

name: sin
summary: Sine of an angle given in degrees
description: Returns the sine of `angle`, where `angle` is in **degrees** (not radians). The result is between -1 and 1. The conversion to radians is done in single precision, so values that should be exactly zero are not: `math.sin(180)` is about -8.7e-8.
notes: Takes degrees, not radians — multiply a 0..1 cycle by 360 for a full wave.
`math.sin(180)` and `math.sin(360)` are tiny negatives, not 0; `math.floor(math.sin(180))` is -1.
The last bit can differ between platforms, since the game uses the device's C library for this.

name: sqrt
summary: Square root
description: Returns the square root of `value`. A negative input gives NaN — and NaN counts as *true* in conditions.
notes: `math.sqrt(-1) ? 1 : 2` is 1: only an exact 0 is false in Molang, and NaN is not 0.

name: trunc
summary: Drop the fractional part, rounding toward zero
description: Returns `value` with its fractional part removed, rounding toward zero: `math.trunc(1.9)` is 1 and `math.trunc(-1.9)` is -1.
notes: Differs from `math.floor` for negative input.
